concept.name: Out-of-the-money option
concept.definition: An out-of-the-money (OTM) option is an option with no intrinsic value: a call whose strike is above the current underlying price, or a put whose strike is below it. Its premium consists entirely of time value, and it expires worthless if still OTM at expiration.
concept.intuition: An OTM option is a lottery-like claim: cheap, but it only pays if the underlying moves far enough before time runs out.
concept.mechanics: OTM options have small absolute deltas, lower premiums, and percentage-wise high sensitivity to volatility. The CFTC glossary example: a call with a $400 strike on gold trading at $390 is $10 out-of-the-money.
concept.formula: Intrinsic value = 0; premium = time value only.
concept.failure_modes: Most OTM options expire worthless, so repeated buying of cheap OTM options bleeds capital; conversely, OTM sellers face gap risk — a sudden large move can convert small premium income into large losses. Skew means OTM equity puts are often relatively expensive.
concept.misconceptions: 'Cheap' OTM options are not necessarily good value: their price already embeds the market's implied probability of the required move, and the probability-weighted expected payoff is typically less than the premium after costs.
concept.example: With stock at $100, the $110 call is OTM and might trade at $0.40; unless the stock exceeds $110 at expiration it expires worthless and the buyer loses the $40 per contract.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
